units.translation: c. Cyrene is said to have been: many have recorded that Apollo, seeing Cyrene, daughter of Hypseus, by the Peneius, brought her to Libya, where he had intercourse with her, where also the city Cyrene was founded, and he begot Aristaeus. Some say Cyrene was daughter of Peneius, others of Hypseus son of Peneius. L
d. πέφαται: is said, is related. Lg P
e. Αἱμονίης: of Thessaly, from Haemon son of Ares.
f. χϑονίης: to the native women. Lg P
g. Μυρτώσιον 〈αἶπος〉: a place near Cyrene or a headland. Lg P
h. Ἀγρέα καὶ Νόμιον: 〈Agreus,〉 because Apollo had intercourse with his mother in the field;
Nomius, because he had intercourse with his mother while she was pasturing; others, because he introduced the care of the fields to the shepherds.
i. μακραίωνα: long-lived. Lg (P)
k. καὶ ἀγρότιν: because she was fond of hunting. For it is related that in Libya, when Eurypylus was king, she subdued a lion.
l. 〈ἀεξηϑέντι:〉 having grown. Lg
m. ἀκεστορίην τε ϑεοπρο〈πίας〉: for they say that he was taught medicine and prophecy by the Muses and took Autonoe as wife, clearly the daughter of Cadmus.
n. ϑέσαν ἤρανον: and the Muses made him guardian of their own flocks. The Athamantian plain is so called around Halus; for Athamas dwelt in Halus, having left the island of his kingdom.
o. Othrys is a high mountain of Thessaly, and the Apidanus is a river of Thessaly.
p. Μινωΐδας: he means the Cyclades, since Minos, being a Cretan, ruled over the islands, mastering the sea, having driven out the Carians.
q. Σείριος: either from the boiling heat, Seirios and seirios. Or from

the fact that it empties us as we flow with sweat; for siron means to empty. Or it is the cause of grinning; at any rate it makes dogs grin and gape. Or from being shaken and quivering. Similarly they call all the stars seiria, as being teirea, signs for sailors; the astrologers, however, call the bright stars that are in motion 〈thus〉. Some say the star is the dog of Orion, others of Erigone, others of Alcyoneus, others of Isis, others of Cephalus, others that it is a proper name, as Timosthenes (fg 42 E. A. Wagner Die Erdbeschreibung des T., Diss. Lips. 1888, 73) says.
r. 〈Κέῳ:〉 Cos is an island, whence Hippocrates came. Lg
s. Παρράσιον λαόν: Arcadian, from one city, Parrhasia. Lg (P)
t. Διὸς Ἰκμαίοιο: for the sake of moisture. In Ceos there is a sanctuary of Zeus Icmaios, that is, of the moist, since he is the cause of the blowing of the winds.
u. τοῖο δ’ ἕκητι: for the sake of Zeus. Lg (P)
